analysis.title: US Watch: October CPI Inflation: Opening the Door to a 50bp Hike in December
key_insights: October CPI was the third straight upside surprise. Headline CPI rose 0.4% m/m and core rose 0.3% m/m.
BofA now tracks October core PCE at 0.32% m/m (3.3% y/y), up from its initial estimate of 0.23% m/m.
BofA says the data all but lock in a December hike. Gov. Waller's hawkish comments the same morning open the door to a 50bp move.

The distribution of CPI components has shifted to the right. More categories contribute above their historical averages and fewer contribute below, which BofA reads as a fading disinflationary impulse and broader inflation firmness.

Core goods rose 0.2% m/m despite a sharp drop in used car prices, and run at a 2.1% annualized pace over three months. Electronics are a major contributor, potentially reflecting AI-related demand and higher input costs.

Core services rose 0.3% m/m and run at a 4.2% annualized pace over three months. Core services ex rents ran at 5.5% 3-month annualized in October versus 1.0% in July, driven largely by airfares and lodging.

BofA says October is the last CPI report before the December Fed meeting and another hot print takes a hold off the table. It keeps its call for a 25bp hike, sees the Fed falling behind the curve, and calls the October hold a likely policy mistake.
BofA sees rising risk that the Fed has to hike again in January rather than March.

The 1y inflation swap rate was about 8bp higher than Monday's close at 2.05% in early post-print trading, so the market does not expect the upside surprise to reverse. This supports BofA's bias toward flattening the nominal curve.

The 'real Sofr' 2s10s curve is inverted 11bp but is priced to steepen 31bp to +20bp in two years, almost double the steepening priced in the nominal curve. BofA argues the case for real curve flattening is stronger than for nominal.
BofA argues longer-term inflation pricing looks complacent. 5y5y real rates are much higher than after the financial crisis and 5y5y inflation is much lower.

The USD rose roughly 0.25-0.5% against G10 currencies after the print. December Fed pricing moved from +21bp to +29bp. BofA says the USD should stay broadly supported, while potential Iran de-escalation (oil lower) and AI regulation uncertainty (weighing on US tech) have held it back.

trade_ideas.description: Bias toward flattening the nominal US curve, with real Sofr curve flattening favored even more strongly
trade_ideas.rationale: The real Sofr 2s10s curve is priced to steepen 31bp in two years, almost double the nominal curve steepening, while longer-term inflation pricing looks complacent.
trade_ideas.risk: BofA says it would not want to wildly extrapolate one month's inflation print.

risk_factors: Another hot CPI print would take a December hold off the table.
The Fed may be falling behind the curve on inflation, raising the risk of a second hike in January rather than March.
Goods and services inflation are both accelerating, and breadth of inflation is widening.
Longer-term inflation expectations may be too low, leaving inflation pricing vulnerable.
A potential Iran de-escalation and AI regulation uncertainty are holding back the USD.

tension_points.bull_case: BofA's base case is a 25bp hike in December, though it sees rising risk of another hike in January rather than March.
tension_points.bear_case: Gov. Waller opened the door to a 50bp hike, contingent on the upside CPI print, and BofA says the Fed seems to be falling behind the curve.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Another hot CPI print takes a December hold off the table. BofA names October CPI as the last report before the December meeting.
